title: Effect of performance level on pacing strategy during a 10-km running race
authors: Lima-Silva AE, Bertuzzi RC, Pires FO, Barros RV, Gagliardi JF, Hammond J, Kiss MA, Bishop DJ
population: 24 male runners in a self-paced treadmill 10-km trial, split into terciles by performance (high and low groups compared)
findings: In the high-performing (HP) group velocity peaked at 18.8 +/- 1.4 km/h in the first 400 m, above the HP average race velocity (P < 0.05), then fell until 2,000 m (P < 0.05), stayed constant until 9,600 m and rose again at the end (P < 0.05).

The low-performing (LP) group ran the first 400 m at 15.6 +/- 1.6 km/h, a significantly lower velocity than HP; this was not different from the LP average race velocity (14.5 +/- 0.7 km/h). LP velocity then fell non-significantly until 9,600 m and rose at the end (P < 0.05).
High and low performance runners adopted different pacing strategies; peak treadmill velocity, running economy and lactate threshold correlated with start, middle, last and average velocity.
limitations: 24 men on a treadmill, not a road race; terciles of one small sample; the abstract prints 'P > 0.05' beside the HP versus LP start velocity while its text says significantly lower, read here as the text states it.
implications: Laboratory 10 km pacing: the better runners opened above their own average, slowed to 2,000 m and held to 9,600 m; both groups rose at the end, and the slower group did not open above its own average. It does not support a prescribed 10 km split pattern. Kept as the 10 km counterpart of the road-race pacing records, with the limit that it is a treadmill study.
